criteria.descriptor: Full marks require correct, true claims throughout: the ~16 bytes/param full-FT figure with the components named and the point that optimizer/master states dominate; ~0.5 byte/param for the 4-bit base; on-the-fly dequantization of a frozen NF4 base to the bf16 compute dtype; gradients flowing only to A and B with the base receiving none; the alpha/r scaling and zero-init of B; all-linear-layer targeting; and the merge-then-requantize mismatch. Deduct for false statements such as the base weights being trained/updated, NF4 being lossless, or alpha setting the parameter count.

Full marks require substantive coverage of all four requested parts: (1) the memory breakdown contrasting full FT with QLoRA, (2) forward/backward behavior and where gradients do and do not flow, (3) rank/alpha/target-module choices with the QLoRA target-module finding, and (4) the deployment merge trade-off including the 4-bit re-quantization wrinkle. Missing or only-gestured parts lose marks proportionally.

Full marks require causal justification rather than assertion: why QLoRA fits (the base's gradients and fp32 optimizer/master states are eliminated), why adapter breadth beats large rank, why zero-init B gives a safe start, and why re-quantizing a merged model injects error the adapter never saw. Answers that merely list facts without the underlying mechanism score lower.

Full marks for a well-organized, design-review-appropriate answer that maps cleanly to the four parts, uses precise terminology (NF4, compute/dequant dtype, alpha/r, adapter merge, paged optimizer) correctly, and stays concise. Rambling, disorganized, or jargon-misusing answers score lower.

expected_answer_points: Full fine-tuning with Adam costs ~16 bytes/param (bf16 weight + bf16 grad + fp32 master + fp32 Adam m,v), ~200 GB for 13B, so it exceeds 24 GB; the optimizer/master states dominate, not the weights themselves.

QLoRA fits because the base is stored in 4-bit NF4 (~0.5 byte/param, ~6.5 GB) and only the tiny adapters carry gradients and optimizer states; gradient checkpointing and a paged optimizer absorb activations/spikes.
The frozen NF4 base is dequantized on the fly to the bf16 compute dtype for each matmul and discarded; NF4 is a lossy 4-bit quantile type, not an exact store.

Gradients flow only to the LoRA matrices A and B (and their optimizer states); the quantized base gets no gradient/no optimizer state, which is the source of the memory saving; B is zero-initialized so training starts at the base model.
r sets adapter capacity/param count while alpha scales the update as alpha/r (e.g. alpha ~ 2r); they are distinct levers.
Per the QLoRA finding, attaching adapters to all linear layers (attention q/k/v/o and MLP gate/up/down) matters more for matching full-FT quality than pushing rank high; breadth beats depth of rank.
Merging folds W + (alpha/r)BA into one matrix to remove adapter inference latency and serve a single model.

Re-quantizing the merged weights to 4-bit introduces a quantization error the adapter never trained against, degrading quality; mitigate by merging into an fp16 base or keeping the adapter unmerged (which also enables multi-adapter hot-swap).
common_pitfalls: Claims QLoRA's saving comes mainly from shrinking the base weights to 4-bit, missing that the dominant saving is removing the gradients and fp32 Adam/master states for the frozen base.
States or implies the 4-bit base weights are updated during training, rather than only the A and B adapter matrices.
Treats adapter merging as always free and lossless, ignoring that re-quantizing the merged weights to 4-bit introduces error the adapter never trained against.
Recommends maximizing rank r as the primary quality lever, overlooking the QLoRA finding that attaching adapters to all linear layers matters more than large rank.
Confuses alpha with rank, or claims alpha sets the number of trainable parameters, when alpha only scales the update via the alpha/r factor.
Believes NF4 stores weights exactly or that dequantization recovers the original bf16 values, rather than being lossy quantile quantization of normally distributed weights.
reference_answer:
1) Memory. Mixed-precision full fine-tuning with Adam costs roughly 16 bytes/parameter: a bf16 weight (2) + bf16 gradient (2) + an fp32 master copy (4) + fp32 Adam m and v (4+4). For 13B that is ~208 GB before activations, far beyond 24 GB; the optimizer/master states, not the weights, dominate. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4 (~0.5 byte/param -> ~6.5 GB, less with double quantization) and only the small LoRA adapters (<1% of params) carry gradients and Adam states, so those cost a few hundred MB. The rest of the budget is activations, cut with gradient checkpointing, plus a paged optimizer that offloads spikes to CPU. It fits.

2) Forward/backward. NF4 is a lossy 4-bit quantile ('NormalFloat') type tuned for zero-centered normal weights. The base is frozen: on each matmul its NF4 weights are dequantized on the fly to the bf16 compute dtype, used, then discarded. The LoRA path runs alongside: h = W_deq x + (alpha/r)·B(Ax), with A,B in bf16 and B initialized to zero (A Gaussian) so at step 0 the adapter is a no-op and training starts exactly at the base model. Backprop computes gradients only for A and B; the quantized base receives no gradient and no optimizer state - that is the whole saving. W_deq is still used to propagate gradients to earlier activations, but dW is never accumulated.

3) Hyperparameters. r (commonly 8-64) sets adapter capacity/param count; alpha enters as the scale alpha/r, so it amplifies the update independent of r (set alpha ~ 2r, then tune). Crucially, the QLoRA paper found that matching full-FT quality depends on attaching adapters to all linear layers (q,k,v,o plus the MLP gate/up/down), not just q and v - the breadth of adapted matrices matters more than a large rank. So prefer many modules at modest rank over few modules at high rank.

4) Merge trade-off. For inference you can fold W_merged = W + (alpha/r)·BA into one matrix, removing the extra adapter matmul and serving a single model. The wrinkle: the adapter was trained to correct one specific NF4-quantized base. If you dequantize, add BA, then re-quantize the merged weights back to 4-bit, you inject a new quantization error the adapter never saw, degrading quality. Mitigate by merging into an fp16/bf16 base (serve in fp16/8-bit, higher memory) or by keeping the adapter unmerged at inference - which also lets you hot-swap multiple adapters on one dequantized base at a small latency cost.
